client: I’ve been really struggling with my classes this semester. No matter how much I try, I feel like I’m always falling behind, and it’s making me so anxious that I’ve stopped hanging out with my friends. I just don’t know how to tell them I’m failing without feeling ashamed.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy burden of pressure and isolation right now, and I hear how painful that feels. I wonder if we could explore together what thoughts come up when you imagine telling your friends about your struggles? What do you worry might happen if you were honest with them?

client: I keep imagining them thinking I'm stupid or lazy. Like they'll realize I'm not as smart as they thought I was, and then they won't want to hang out with me anymore. It's stupid because these are my closest friends, but the fear feels so real.
therapist: Those thoughts must feel so overwhelming, and yet I notice you're also recognizing that this fear might not match the reality of your close friendships. What would it be like to consider that your friends might actually respond with care and support if they knew how much you're struggling?

client: I guess logically I know they'd probably be supportive, but it's like my brain keeps showing me worst-case scenarios. Last month when Sarah was struggling with her breakup, we all helped her - but for some reason I can't imagine getting that same kindness in return.
therapist: It's interesting how clearly you can see the kindness you showed Sarah, yet struggle to imagine receiving it yourself - that disconnect must feel really lonely. What do you think might be different about how you view others' struggles versus your own?

client: I think I'm way harder on myself than I am on my friends. Like when Sarah was upset, I just wanted to help her feel better, but when it's me struggling, I feel like I should be able to handle everything perfectly. It's exhausting holding myself to this impossible standard.
therapist: You've made such an important observation about these double standards you're holding - that must feel both enlightening and exhausting to recognize. How might it feel to experiment with treating yourself with the same compassion you so easily offer your friends?

client: It sounds nice in theory, but I don't even know how to start being kinder to myself. Every time I try, this voice in my head just says I'm making excuses for being lazy. Maybe I don't deserve the same compassion because my problems are about school, not something big like a breakup.
therapist: That critical voice sounds so loud and persistent - no wonder self-compassion feels out of reach right now. What would it be like to notice that voice without believing it, like observing a radio playing in another room?

client: That actually makes me feel a little lighter - like maybe the voice doesn't have to control me. But it's scary because that critical voice has been driving me to study so hard. If I stop listening to it, won't I just fall even further behind?
therapist: It makes so much sense that you'd worry about losing your motivation if that critical voice quiets down - it's been your driving force for so long. What if we explored kinder, more sustainable ways to stay motivated that don't leave you feeling so exhausted and isolated?

client: I'd like to try that, but I don't even know what kinder motivation would look like. All I've ever known is beating myself up until I get things done. The idea of being nice to myself while studying feels... wrong somehow, like I'm not taking it seriously enough.
therapist: It sounds like being kind to yourself feels almost dangerous when it comes to academic performance - like letting up on the pressure might mean everything will fall apart. Could we explore what might happen if you experimented with studying while speaking to yourself the way you'd encourage a close friend?

client: I tried that once and immediately felt guilty, like I was cheating or something. It's weird because when my friend Mark was prepping for exams last year, I kept telling him "You've got this" and "Take breaks when you need to" - but when I say those same things to myself, they feel like lies.
therapist: You've noticed such an important pattern - how the same words feel true when said to others but somehow false when directed at yourself. What do you think that gap might be protecting you from, or what might it be trying to prevent?

client: Maybe it's protecting me from... disappointment? If I expect the worst from myself, then I can't be let down. But when I'm kind to my friends, I don't worry about them failing - I just want to support them. It's confusing why I can't apply that same trust to myself.
therapist: You've uncovered something really profound here - the way expecting the worst might feel safer than risking disappointment. I wonder what it would be like to experiment with holding onto that trust you so easily extend to your friends, even if just in small ways?

client: I could try trusting myself a little, but what if I start believing I can do better and then still fail? That would hurt way more than just expecting the worst from the start. It's like I'd rather be right about being a failure than wrong about being capable.
therapist: That fear of hoping and then falling short feels so vulnerable, doesn't it? I wonder what it might be like to hold both possibilities - that you *could* succeed *and* that setbacks wouldn't define your worth, just as they don't define your friends' worth when they struggle?
